svg.text: VGA's five sub-chips — a small network, not one device
CRTC, Sequencer, Graphics Controller, Attribute Controller, and DAC, each with its own I/O ports and register set, wired to a shared bank of video RAM
reading status port 0x3DA unconditionally clears the AC's index/data flip-flop
— an electrical coupling between two "unrelated" blocks, not a software design choice
SHARED VIDEO RAM — 4 planes x 64 KB, mapped at segment 0xA000
planar layout: one byte address selects the same offset in all four planes at once
solid lines = wired directly to VRAM (CRTC's scanout address, Sequencer's plane mask, GC's write-mode transform)
dashed lines = downstream of VRAM in the scanout pipeline, not direct writers (Attribute Controller, DAC — see below)
scanout pixel pipeline — one pixel at a time, not one CPU byte at a time
CRTC's raster timing paces every step of this pipeline
Three of the five blocks share one access pattern: an index port picks a register, a data port writes it
CRTC, Sequencer, and Graphics Controller each use this index/data pair; the Attribute Controller collapses it into one port
and the DAC uses three ports because a color needs three consecutive byte writes (red, then green, then blue)
on real 1987 silicon these were separate manufactured components on one PCB — the register map was the only thing holding the network together
each I/O port above has its own entry in DOSBox-X's flat io_writehandlers table (Chapter 2, §2.4) — this diagram omits the read-side ports
